migrationNotes: Spine: take a gardener's claim that fertiliser helps plants and put it through the decisions of a fair test in turn: what to measure, how to compare plants that start at different sizes, a control and random assignment, replicate pots and their spread. It ends with a survey of ponds, where nobody assigned the cause.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): bio-ecological-evidence-2 and -change-why. The change from a baseline is taught on the second screen and asked through the opening plants (-hook). New item bio-ecological-evidence-mean (mean of three pots) gives the replicate screen a practice question before the skill check.

lesson.title: What counts as evidence

lead.text: A claim such as “fertiliser makes plants grow better” cannot be tested as it stands, because “better” can stand for different things to different people. To test it we choose an outcome, the thing we will measure to see whether the claim holds. A good outcome can be recorded with an instrument and written down as a number, and anyone repeating the test would measure it the same way.

Take a different claim as practice: “this lamp keeps seedlings healthier”. “Healthier” is a judgement, but the number of seedlings still alive after two weeks is a count, and the width of a leaf in millimetres is a measurement. Either would do, as long as we pick one before we start and keep to it. Choosing afterwards, whichever looks best, would let us find what we hoped to find. The gardener's claim is about growth, so her outcome has to be a number that records how much a plant has grown over a fixed time.
The gardener wants a measurement that records growth over a set time.

The gardener's two plants did not start at the same size, and that matters. Compare two seedlings, P and Q, over three weeks. P starts at 6 cm and finishes at 15 cm. Q starts at 10 cm and finishes at 17 cm. Q is taller at the end, but it was also taller at the start. A plant's starting measurement is its baseline, and what we want is the change from the baseline, which is the final height minus the baseline.
P grew 15 − 6 = 9 cm and Q grew 17 − 10 = 7 cm, so P grew more even though Q finished taller.

afterFigure.text: A final height mixes two things together: how big the plant already was and how much it grew. Subtracting the baseline removes the first and leaves the growth, which is what a fertiliser is supposed to change. For that reason we compare changes from baseline and not final sizes. The figure plots both seedlings week by week.

lead.text: Use the two plants from the start of the lesson. They began at different heights, just as P and Q did.

steps.headline: A control and a fair draw

lead.text: Growth on its own still proves little, because plants grow with or without fertiliser. We need something to compare the treated plants against. A control group is treated in every way the same except for the one thing being tested. In the gardener's test the control pots get plain water instead of fertiliser and have the same light and soil as the others. If the treated group grows 12 cm and the control 8 cm, the apparent effect of the fertiliser is the difference, 12 − 8 = 4 cm.

afterFigure.text: The groups also have to start out alike. If the gardener chooses by hand which pots get the fertiliser, she may put the pots nearest the window in the treated group without meaning to, and they would grow more because of the extra light. The remedy is random assignment: give each pot to a group by chance, with a coin or a shuffled pack of cards, so that differences in light, size and soil are spread over both groups.

lead.text: The pots are alike, and the gardener has to split them into two groups.
Compare the two groups over the same three weeks.

One treated pot and one control pot can still mislead, because individual plants vary. One seed may be weak, or one pot may drain badly. To see how much results vary, the test needs replicates: separate pots, each treated independently. Measuring the same pot ten times is not replication, since it only tells you more about that one pot.

With several pots we report the mean, which is the total of the growths divided by the number of pots. Three control pots that grow 5, 8 and 11 cm have a mean of (5 + 8 + 11) ÷ 3 = 8 cm. Three that grow 7, 8 and 9 cm also have a mean of 8 cm, but they tell a different story, because the first set is spread widely and the second sits close together. How far results are spread is their variability. A mean on its own can hide wide differences between pots, and a small gap between the treated and control means is hard to trust when the pots within each group differ a lot.
Share the total growth equally between the pots.

An experiment lets the experimenter decide which plants get the treatment. A survey does not. In a survey we go out and measure what is already there. Suppose surveyors visit 40 ponds and find that the ponds with more reeds also have more frogs. That is an association: the two rise and fall together. It is a fair reason to suspect that reeds help frogs, perhaps by giving them shelter, so it gives us a hypothesis worth testing.

afterFigure.text: An association does not show a cause by itself, because nobody assigned the reeds. Something else could lie behind both. In the figure the frogs rise with the reeds in sunny ponds and in shaded ones, yet the shaded ponds hold fewer frogs at every reed cover, so something other than reeds, such as light, matters too. To show that reeds cause the difference you would need an experiment that adds reeds to some ponds chosen at random and keeps the others as controls.

lead.text: Surveyors measure plants at many sites and find taller plants at the wetter ones. Nobody assigned the rainfall: this is an observation, not an experiment.

lesson.orientation: Design fair ecological comparisons and avoid turning correlation into an unsupported cause.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A gardener says that fertiliser makes plants grow taller, and she sets out to show it. One seedling gets fertiliser. It starts at 4 cm and after three weeks it stands at 19 cm. A second seedling gets none. It starts at 12 cm and after three weeks it stands at 22 cm. At the end the unfed plant is the taller one.

That looks bad for the fertiliser, but two plants cannot settle anything. A fair test has to decide what to measure and how to compare plants that start at different sizes. It also has to decide which plants get the treatment and how many plants to use.

The last two lessons used numbers that someone had to measure. This lesson follows the gardener's claim through those decisions one at a time, and ends with what a pattern seen in the wild can and cannot show.

intro.promise: By the end you'll judge whether a plant experiment is fair, and say what an observed pattern can and cannot show.

recap.keyIdea: A fair test compares the change from baseline in a treated group and a control, assigns plants to groups by chance and uses independent replicates. A survey on its own shows an association and cannot show a cause.

blocks.text: You compared how much plants grew and set that against how tall they ended up, and you found a treated group 3 cm ahead of its control. You took the mean of three pots and saw why a mean needs its spread. You also saw why more frogs among more reeds does not prove that reeds are the cause.

recap.nextHook: That completes the course. You have followed living things from the parts of a cell to the pond around a heron, and the habit of asking what was measured and how it was compared applies to every claim along the way.

questions.prompt: A claim says fertiliser helps plants grow. Name the quantity you would measure to test it.
hints: Choose something you can measure with a ruler over a set time.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A defined measurable outcome, such as change in height over a set time, allows a reproducible comparison.

questions.onCorrect: Height, or its change over a set time. A measurable outcome makes the claim testable.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a judgement, not a measurement. Pick something you could record with a ruler.

questions.prompt: Group A grows from 10 cm to 16 cm. How much does its mean height increase, in cm?
hints: Use the same group's baseline.
Subtract the starting height from the final height.
Take the starting height off the final height.
questions.onCorrect: 6 cm. Growth is the final height minus the baseline.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the final height. Subtract the starting height.
That adds the heights. Growth is the change, so subtract.

questions.prompt: Comparable pots are allocated to fertiliser or control by chance. Name this allocation method.
hints: Name how treatments are given out, not how often height is measured.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Random assignment reduces systematic group differences; independent pots provide replication.

questions.onCorrect: Random assignment. Chance spreads other differences evenly between the groups.

misconceptions.feedback: Replication means using many independent pots. This question asks how treatments are given out.

questions.prompt: Taller plants occur at wetter sites. What follows from that observation alone?
hints: A correlation does not isolate a cause.

acceptedIdeas: Rainfall and height are associated, but other causes need checking
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The association could reflect rainfall, soil or other related factors.

choices.label: Rainfall is proven to be the only cause
Rainfall and height are associated, but other causes need checking

questions.onCorrect: The two are associated. Other factors, such as soil, could explain the pattern.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing was controlled, so other causes cannot be ruled out.
Nothing links plant height to rainfall in that direction.

questions.prompt: A treated group increases by 9 cm and its control group by 6 cm over the same interval. What is the difference in growth, in cm?
hints: Compare changes over the same interval.
Use growth, not final height.
Subtract the control's growth from the treated group's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9 − 6 = 3 cm greater growth in the treated group.

questions.onCorrect: 3 cm. Subtract the control's growth to see the effect of the treatment.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two growths. Compare them by subtracting.
That is the treated group's growth alone. Take the control's growth away.

questions.prompt: Why report variability across independent pots as well as the mean?
hints: An average alone does not show the spread.

acceptedIdeas: It shows how consistent the results are
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Variability reveals whether the mean hides wide differences between replicates.

choices.label: It shows how consistent the results are
It proves every plant behaves identically

questions.onCorrect: It shows how consistent the results are. A mean can hide wide differences between pots.

misconceptions.feedback: A control is still needed to compare against. Variability tells you about consistency.
Variability shows the opposite: how much the plants differ.

questions.prompt: Three independent treated pots grow 7 cm, 9 cm and 11 cm. What is the mean growth, in cm?
hints: Add the three growths.
Divide the total by the number of pots.
Share the total equally between the pots.
questions.onCorrect: 9 cm. The mean is the total divided by the number of independent pots.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total. Divide it by the number of pots.
That is the largest value. The mean uses every pot.

questions.prompt: A researcher gives fertiliser only to the plants that already look healthiest. Name the feature of a fair test that this breaks.
hints: How should treatments be given out?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Choosing the healthiest plants for the treatment builds a systematic difference into the groups.

questions.onCorrect: Random assignment. Picking the healthiest plants builds in a difference that has nothing to do with the fertiliser.

misconceptions.feedback: There may still be a control. The problem is how the plants were chosen for each group.
The number of plants is not the problem. The choice of which get the treatment is.

questions.prompt: Plant A, with fertiliser, grows from 4 cm to 19 cm. Plant B, without it, grows from 12 cm to 22 cm. How many more centimetres did plant A grow than plant B?
hints: Growth is the change in height, not the final height.
Work out each plant's growth separately.
Subtract plant B's growth from plant A's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Plant A grew 19 − 4 = 15 cm. Plant B grew 22 − 12 = 10 cm. The difference is 5 cm.

questions.onCorrect: 5 cm. Compare how much each plant grew, because the plants did not start at the same height.

misconceptions.feedback: That compares the final heights, but B ended taller. Compare how much each plant grew.
That is plant A's growth alone. Subtract plant B's growth from it.

questions.prompt: Why compare each group's change instead of its final height?
hints: Think about where each group began.

acceptedIdeas: The groups started at different heights
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Groups that start at different heights can mislead if only final height is compared.

choices.label: The groups started at different heights
Change is always larger than final height

questions.onCorrect: The groups started at different heights, so only each group's change shows how much it grew.

misconceptions.feedback: Final heights can be measured. They just do not show how much each group grew.
Size does not decide which measure is fairer. The starting point does.

questions.prompt: Three independent control pots grow 3 cm, 6 cm and 12 cm. What is the mean growth, in cm?
hints: Add the three growths.
Divide the total by the number of pots.
Share the total equally between the pots.
questions.onCorrect: 7 cm. The mean is the total growth divided by the number of independent pots.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total. Divide it by the number of pots.
That is the largest value. The mean uses every pot.
That is the middle pot. The mean uses every pot, not only the middle one.
